title: NCSA Mosaic 1.0 Released
summary: NCSA Mosaic 1.0 was released for Unix, Windows, and Mac, making the web accessible to millions.
narrative: On April 22, 1993, NCSA released Mosaic 1.0 for free download. Within weeks, it was the most popular program on the internet. For the first time, ordinary people could browse the web with a point-and-click interface. Images loaded right alongside text, and navigating was as simple as clicking blue underlined words. The web had its killer app.
why_it_matters: Mosaic brought the web to the masses and established the browser as the primary interface to the internet.
image_caption: NCSA Mosaic 1.0 was released for Unix, Windows, and Mac, making the web accessible to millions.

title: GIF89a Animation Standard Released
summary: The GIF89a specification introduced animation support, enabling the animated GIFs that would define internet culture.
narrative: The original GIF format was useful but static. GIF89a changed everything by adding animation support—multiple images stored in one file, playing in sequence. This simple addition would create an entire internet culture of animated memes, dancing baby GIFs, and eventually the reaction GIFs that dominate social media today. It was a small technical update with enormous cultural consequences.
why_it_matters: Animated GIFs became a universal language of internet expression, from memes to reaction images.
image_caption: The GIF89a specification introduced animation support, enabling the animated GIFs that would define internet culture.

title: Windows 3.1 Released
summary: Microsoft released Windows 3.1, the most popular operating system of the early 1990s.
narrative: Windows 3.1 wasn't just an operating system—it was a cultural phenomenon. With its Solitaire game, Minesweeper, and colorful interface, it brought computing to millions of homes. For many, this was their first experience with a graphical user interface. The sound of its startup chime became the soundtrack of the early 90s.
why_it_matters: Windows 3.1 established Microsoft's dominance in personal computing and prepared millions for the internet age.
image_caption: Microsoft released Windows 3.1, the most popular operating system of the early 1990s.

title: University of Minnesota Charges for Gopher
summary: The University of Minnesota announced it would charge licensing fees for Gopher, accelerating its decline.
narrative: Gopher was the web's biggest competitor until the University of Minnesota made a fatal mistake: they announced they would charge licensing fees for Gopher servers. In a world built on free and open protocols, this was seen as a betrayal. Users and administrators abandoned Gopher en masse for the free and open World Wide Web. The decision accelerated the web's dominance.
why_it_matters: This decision pushed users toward the open web, demonstrating that free standards would win on the internet.
image_caption: The University of Minnesota announced it would charge licensing fees for Gopher, accelerating its decline.

title: First Web Comics Published
summary: Early web comics began appearing online, pioneering digital storytelling.
narrative: Artists were among the first to see the web's creative potential. In 1993, the first web comics appeared—simple image files linked together with navigation. These digital comics demonstrated that the web could be a creative medium, not just an information repository. They would eventually evolve into a massive industry with works like XKCD and Homestar Runner.
why_it_matters: Web comics proved that the web could be a creative platform, inspiring generations of digital artists.
image_caption: Early web comics began appearing online, pioneering digital storytelling.

title: First Online Gambling Site
summary: The first internet gambling sites began operating, pioneering online gaming.
narrative: Before online casinos became a billion-dollar industry, a few pioneering sites began offering gambling over the internet. Using simple interfaces and email-based transactions, these early sites demonstrated that people would gamble online. The legal and regulatory battles that followed would shape internet commerce for decades.
why_it_matters: Online gambling pioneered secure online transactions and raised fundamental questions about internet regulation.
image_caption: The first internet gambling sites began operating, pioneering online gaming.

title: First Web Directories Emerge
summary: The first human-curated web directories appeared, helping users navigate the growing web.
narrative: As the web grew from hundreds to thousands of pages, people needed help finding things. The first web directories—hand-curated lists of websites organized by category—began appearing. These directories were the web's first search engines, albeit maintained by humans rather than algorithms. They would inspire Yahoo!, DMOZ, and the entire search industry.
why_it_matters: Web directories established the concept of organizing web content, leading to search engines and SEO.
image_caption: The first human-curated web directories appeared, helping users navigate the growing web.

title: InterNIC Established for Domain Management
summary: InterNIC was established to manage domain name registration, professionalizing the DNS system.
narrative: As domain names became valuable property, the internet needed organized management. InterNIC took over domain registration from the government, creating a professional system for managing the .com, .org, and .net namespaces. This was the beginning of domain names as a business, and the foundation for the domain gold rush of the late 90s.
why_it_matters: InterNIC professionalized domain management and established the infrastructure for the domain name industry.
image_caption: InterNIC was established to manage domain name registration, professionalizing the DNS system.

title: Mosaic Featured in Major Media
summary: NCSA Mosaic received widespread media coverage, bringing the web to public attention.
narrative: The New York Times ran a front-page story on Mosaic, and suddenly everyone was talking about the World Wide Web. The browser that had been popular in academic circles was now a cultural phenomenon. Download requests skyrocketed as curious non-technical users tried the web for the first time. The internet had entered the mainstream consciousness.
why_it_matters: Media coverage brought the web to mainstream awareness and attracted the investment that would fuel the dot-com boom.
image_caption: NCSA Mosaic received widespread media coverage, bringing the web to public attention.

title: CERN Puts the World Wide Web into the Public Domain
summary: CERN made the World Wide Web source code available on a royalty-free basis forever.
narrative: Had CERN decided to patent and license the World Wide Web software, the web as we know it would likely not exist. Instead, CERN directors and Tim Berners-Lee signed a historic declaration placing the underlying code into the public domain with no royalties or fees. This single decision made it risk-free for developers, hobbyists, and universities around the globe to build browsers and host websites without paying a cent.
why_it_matters: This is widely celebrated as the single most consequential legal decision in internet history, guaranteeing the open architecture of the web.

title: id Software Releases DOOM: 3D Gaming & LAN Deathmatches
summary: John Carmack and John Romero released DOOM via shareware, bringing university computer networks to a screeching halt.
narrative: Uploaded to an FTP server at the University of Wisconsin at midnight, DOOM's first episode was free to copy and distribute. With texture-mapped 3D lighting, visceral shotgun combat, and peer-to-peer four-player LAN 'deathmatches', it became an instant international addiction. System administrators at Intel and universities had to write custom scripts just to purge DOOM network packets from their clogged servers.
why_it_matters: DOOM pioneered first-person 3D game engines, shareware viral distribution, user-created mods (WADs), and multiplayer competitive gaming.
image_caption: John Carmack and John Romero released DOOM via shareware, bringing university computer networks to a screeching halt.

title: Jurassic Park Ushers in the Photorealistic CGI Era
summary: Steven Spielberg and ILM amazed the world with computer-generated dinosaurs, transforming Hollywood cinema forever.
narrative: When paleontologist Alan Grant took off his sunglasses to gaze upon a living, breathing digital Brachiosaurus grazing in the canopy, audiences around the world gasped in unison. Industrial Light & Magic's Dennis Muren proved that Silicon Graphics computers could render lifelike living creatures with skin weight and lighting. Stop-motion animator Phil Tippett famously whispered, 'I think I'm extinct.'
why_it_matters: Jurassic Park proved computer graphics could carry emotional narrative weight, setting the gold standard for visual effects for the next three decades.
image_caption: Steven Spielberg and ILM amazed the world with computer-generated dinosaurs, transforming Hollywood cinema forever.
